sections.title: General Considerations
sections.body: In most cases, spread footings represent the most economical foundation type if they do not have to be installed deeply into the ground. At some limiting depth, a 'shallow' foundation begins to behave like and have the associated construction needs of a 'deep' foundation. This limiting depth is somewhat arbitrary but generally can be taken as about two times the least-plan dimension of the foundation. The decision to use a shallow foundation for support of a structure includes checking that an adequate margin of safety is provided against failure of the ground below the bearing depth (bearing capacity failure), and checking that deformations (settlement) under expected loading conditions will be acceptable. Design checks will also be performed to make sure the footing will not slide and that it is stable (e.g., will not overturn). If the foundation can meet these fundamental design requirements, it also must be constructible. Constructability considerations are discussed in Section 3.3.
key_points: Spread footings are generally the most economical foundation type if not installed deeply
Limiting depth for 'shallow' behavior is approximately 2 times the least-plan dimension
Design must check bearing capacity, settlement, sliding, and overturning stability
Deformations under expected loading must be within acceptable limits
Constructability is a critical consideration (see Section 3.3)
sections.applicability: Initial foundation type selection for all transportation structures where shallow foundations are being considered.

sections.title: Footings on Cohesionless Soils
sections.body: Granular, or cohesionless, soils are generally more suited to support of shallow foundations than cohesive soils, particularly when a foundation is supported on a structural fill. Cohesionless soils tend to be less prone to settlement under applied loads. Settlement of cohesionless soils generally occurs rapidly, as loads are applied. Special consideration should be given to situations in which the following conditions may occur or be present: (1) Water table close to or above the foundation bearing elevation - saturated ground conditions will result in reduced effective stresses in the soils supporting the footing and an associated reduction in bearing capacity (see Section 4.4 and Chapter 5); (2) Steep slopes near the bearing elevation of a footing - an adequate factor of safety with respect to global stability must be maintained over the life of the structure; (3) Presence of collapsible soils - collapsible soils are generally stable when dry, but upon wetting or saturation, rapid settlement (collapse) can occur that could exceed the performance (settlement) criteria for the structure; collapsible soils are regional in their occurrence and should be evaluated based on site-specific subsurface data and local knowledge; (4) Presence of seismic hazards - seismic hazards, including liquefaction potential under seismic conditions, should be evaluated; if liquefaction is possible, the dynamic stability of the footing should be checked and the potential for dynamic settlement assessed.
key_points: Cohesionless soils are generally more suited for shallow foundations than cohesive soils
Settlement occurs rapidly as loads are applied (no long-term consolidation)
High water table reduces effective stress and bearing capacity
Global stability must be checked where slopes are near the bearing elevation
Collapsible soils can cause rapid settlement upon wetting; evaluate based on site-specific data and local experience
Seismic hazards including liquefaction potential must be evaluated; check dynamic stability and dynamic settlement
sections.applicability: Shallow foundation design on granular/cohesionless soils, including structural fills, with attention to water table, slope stability, collapsible soils, and seismic hazards.

sections.title: Footings on Cohesive Soils
sections.body: Normally consolidated cohesive soils (clays) will experience consolidation settlement when subjected to an increase in stress such as that applied by a shallow foundation. The consolidation process and the procedure for calculating consolidation settlement are described in Section 5.3. Normally consolidated cohesive soils may also exhibit relatively low shear strength when loaded rapidly (undrained loading condition). Therefore, both the bearing capacity for short- and long-term settlement must be evaluated as part of the preliminary design process when considering support of a shallow foundation on cohesive soils. Because cohesive soils can experience large volume changes due to changes in water content, bridge foundations should not be supported on embankments constructed of such materials. Expansive clays in natural conditions can also experience large volume changes. If clay soils are encountered at a site, the expansive potential should be evaluated as part of the site investigation and laboratory testing program before confirming the suitability of spread footings on the natural clay soils. Additional information on identification of expansive soils can be found in the Subsurface Investigation Workshop Reference Manual (Arman et al., 1997). Lightly overconsolidated cohesive soils (OCR of about 1 to 2) may also experience consolidation settlement in primary (virgin) compression under stresses applied by a spread footing. Serviceability must be checked to ensure total and differential settlements are within the acceptable performance range. Heavily overconsolidated cohesive soils with OCRs greater than about 3 or 4 represent the most suitable cohesive soil conditions for consideration of support of shallow foundations. Heavily overconsolidated clays possess relatively high strength and low compressibility characteristics.
key_points: Normally consolidated clays experience consolidation settlement and may have low undrained shear strength
Both short-term (undrained) and long-term (drained) bearing capacity and settlement must be evaluated
Bridge foundations should NOT be supported on embankments constructed of cohesive materials due to volume change potential
Expansive clay potential must be evaluated during site investigation and lab testing
Lightly overconsolidated soils (OCR 1-2) may settle in primary compression; check serviceability
Heavily overconsolidated soils (OCR > 3-4) are the most suitable cohesive soil conditions for shallow foundations
Heavily OC clays have high strength and low compressibility
sections.applicability: Shallow foundation selection on cohesive soils, with critical distinctions based on overconsolidation ratio (OCR) and volume change potential.

sections.title: Footings on Intermediate Geomaterials (IGMs) and Rock
sections.body: Intermediate geomaterial (IGM) is a term for ground conditions that are dense and stiff enough to no longer be characterized as a 'soil' but are not considered intact 'rock' (O'Neill et al., 1996). IGMs include materials such as glacial till, completely weathered rock, poorly to moderately indurated sediments and chemically cemented materials. These materials may occur as the transition from overburden soil to intact rock. The term IGM is rather broad in its definition and may carry regional connotations. For the purpose of shallow foundation design, IGMs are considered sufficiently strong and stiff that design considerations other than material strength (e.g., overturning potential) will typically govern design. IGMs may demand consideration of rock-like characteristics, such as mass structure and discontinuities. Where an IGM or rock material is at or near the ground surface, the most economical foundation system will usually be a shallow foundation bearing in or on the IGM or rock. Three basic types of shallow foundations on IGMs or rock are shown in Figure 3-1: (a) footing on a relatively horizontal or mildly sloping, stable IGM or rock surface; (b) footing near the crest of an IGM or rock slope requiring detailed consideration of global stability including planar, wedge, sliding and toppling failure mechanisms; (c) footing tied into IGM or rock to resist large horizontal or uplift loads. When designing foundations on IGM or rock slopes, the potential for slope instability is a function of the intact mass strength properties, orientation and condition of unfavorable structure or discontinuities (e.g., bedding, joints, foliations). For foundations requiring resistance to large uplift or lateral loads, socketed deep foundations, micropiles, or ground anchors may be considered (O'Neill & Reese, 1999; Armour et al., 2000; Sabatini et al., 1999). Rock and IGMs must be evaluated for degree of weathering, rock strength, durability, and the orientation and condition of discontinuities. Blasting or undermining by cavities can compromise a rock mass. Heavily overconsolidated IGMs (e.g., glacially overridden lakebed sediments) may possess high intact strength but can lose strength drastically if subjected to adverse stress changes or minimal shearing. Foundation selection on IGM or rock should include early assessment of global stability (including structurally controlled failure mechanisms) and the potential for sinkhole or subterranean cavern collapse.
key_points: IGMs are materials too dense/stiff for 'soil' classification but not intact 'rock' (glacial till, weathered rock, indurated sediments, cemented materials)
IGMs are typically strong enough that overturning or stability governs design rather than material strength
Three foundation configurations on IGM/rock: horizontal bearing, near-slope crest, and tied-in for uplift/lateral loads (Figure 3-1)
Slope stability analysis for IGM/rock must consider planar, wedge, sliding, and toppling failure mechanisms
Evaluate weathering degree, rock strength, durability, and discontinuity orientation and condition
Heavily overconsolidated IGMs may lose strength under adverse stress changes or shearing
Assess potential for sinkhole or subterranean cavern collapse
Deep foundations, micropiles, or ground anchors may be needed for large uplift or lateral loads
sections.applicability: Shallow foundation design on intermediate geomaterials and rock, including assessment of discontinuities, slope stability, and potential for strength loss or cavern collapse.

sections.title: Scour Potential
sections.body: Scour is a hydraulic erosion process that lowers the grade of a water channel or river bed. This erosion is caused by flowing water. Excessive removal of the material around a shallow foundation or undermining of a footing can cause excessive deformation or structure collapse. Foundations for bridges and structures located near rivers, channels and in floodplains should be located below the limits of scour. If the scour depth is too deep for a shallow foundation to be constructed using normal methods, consideration should be given to selection of a deep foundation system for support of the structure. Additional details regarding scour potential evaluation and protection are presented in Section 6.2.2.
key_points: Scour is hydraulic erosion that lowers channel or river bed grade and can undermine foundations
Foundations near rivers, channels, and floodplains must be located below the limits of scour
If scour depth is too deep for a shallow foundation, a deep foundation should be considered
Scour potential evaluation and protection details are in Section 6.2.2
sections.applicability: Foundation type selection for bridges and structures near waterways where scour may undermine shallow foundations.

sections.title: Depth of Influence and Frost Protection
sections.body: Because spread footings have plan dimensions of limited areal extent, the stress induced in the ground mass below the footing will diminish with depth. In general, the ground conditions at a depth greater than about four times the lesser plan dimension of a continuous spread footing will be affected by less than about ten percent of the stresses induced under the footing (2 times the lesser plan dimension for square or nearly square footings). Closely spaced footings can have overlapping zones of influence that combine to produce a zone of influence that extends deeper than these rules of thumb. The procedures in Section 5.3 can be used to calculate the stress at a given depth and location below a spread footing. These stress distributions are used in Chapter 5 for evaluation of bearing capacity and settlement. Presumptive bearing capacities for footings on soils that can be found in the literature are typically not a function of width. This is one reason why presumptive values are not presented in this manual, and also why they should be used with caution, or for preliminary design purposes only. Spread footings should be designed to bear below the frost depth for local conditions, or on materials that are not frost susceptible. Section 6.2.3 contains additional discussion on frost protection. As can be seen from the stress bulbs in Figures 5-9 and 5-10, the depth of stress influence is a function of the width of the footing, and the dimensions therefore play a role in the assessment of settlement and bearing capacity.
key_points: Stress influence extends to approximately 4B below continuous footings and 2B below square footings (where B is the lesser plan dimension), at which depth less than 10% of applied stress remains
Closely spaced footings can have overlapping stress zones that extend the depth of influence
Stress distribution procedures in Section 5.3 are used for bearing capacity and settlement evaluation
Presumptive bearing capacities from literature are not functions of footing width; use with caution or for preliminary design only
Spread footings must bear below the frost depth or on non-frost-susceptible materials
Frost protection is discussed in Section 6.2.3
sections.applicability: Determining the depth of stress influence for settlement and bearing capacity analysis, and establishing minimum embedment depth for frost protection.

sections.title: Geotechnical Criteria in Preliminary Design
sections.body: The geotechnical engineer should provide input to the preliminary design process. At this time there is usually insufficient information about pier locations and bridge length to warrant detailed subsurface information with borings. If no existing subsurface information is available in the area, preliminary borings may be appropriate to gain a general understanding of the subsurface conditions at the site. An assessment of ground conditions based on geologic and site reconnaissance, supplemented with subsurface information (either from existing information or preliminary explorations), is critical to structure layout and configuration. Some key considerations include: (1) Potential soft or weak ground conditions can be identified that will limit the steepness of embankment slopes. For bridges, this may dictate pier locations and overall structure length. (2) Geologic hazards, such as earthquakes, volcanic eruption, flood, tsunami, avalanche, landslides, collapsible ground conditions, expansive soils, liquefaction potential, etc., should be identified. The presence of any of these conditions at a structure site can have significant impact not only on foundation type selection, but also on design, cost and/or construction schedules. (3) Feasible foundation types should be evaluated. There may be sufficient existing information to conclude that shallow foundations are feasible at a site. Early consultation with the geotechnical engineer can help avoid costly redesign, either late in the project development process or during construction.
key_points: Geotechnical input is critical early in the preliminary design process
Preliminary borings may be warranted when no existing subsurface data are available
Geologic and site reconnaissance supplemented with subsurface data informs structure layout
Identify soft/weak ground conditions that may limit embankment slopes and dictate pier locations
Evaluate geologic hazards: earthquakes, floods, landslides, collapsible soils, expansive soils, liquefaction
Assess feasible foundation types early to avoid costly redesign
Early geotechnical consultation saves time and cost in the project development process
sections.applicability: Preliminary design phase of transportation structures where geotechnical input is needed to guide foundation type selection and structure layout.

sections.title: Shoring and Construction Excavation Requirements
sections.body: The design of a spread footing should be both efficient and constructible. Sometimes temporary shoring has to be installed before a spread footing can be constructed. The designer should consider whether shoring will be necessary and how it can be constructed. Key questions a designer should ask prior to selection of a shallow foundation include: (1) Will normal excavation equipment be capable of constructing the footing, or will rock or difficult ground conditions in the excavation require special equipment? The geotechnical engineer should consider the type of equipment necessary for the excavation, based on the results of the geotechnical investigation, and provide sufficient commentary in the geotechnical report for the structural designer and estimator. (2) Will the excavation be stable under the temporary conditions, or will shoring be required to stabilize excavation sidewalls? The geotechnical engineer should consider the maximum slope angles at which the excavation slopes will stand without external support, and evaluate the potential for instability due to zones of weak ground and the location of the ground water table. (3) Will obstructions be encountered? Buried structures, utilities, old pile foundations or boulders can result in contractor claims if provisions are not made for relocation or removal. The geotechnical investigation may or may not disclose the presence of obstructions, but the geotechnical engineer should provide commentary when geologic conditions or knowledge of prior site activities indicates obstructions may be encountered. Existing utility location, including physical confirmation by potholing, should be completed early in design. (4) Will water be encountered in the foundation excavation? Water can pose a problem in construction. If there is a high water table, consideration should be given to the stability of the bottom of the foundation soils just before the footing is placed. Softening or heaving of the bottom should be prevented. In some cases, dewatering and seals may be required. The geotechnical investigation should identify the presence and elevation of the water table below a site, and ground water conditions should be assessed at all times of the year, particularly when there is potential for seasonal variation of the water level.
key_points: Foundation design must consider constructability, not just structural adequacy
Evaluate whether normal excavation equipment is adequate or special equipment is needed for rock or difficult ground
Assess excavation stability and whether shoring is required; consider maximum safe slope angles and weak ground zones
Identify potential obstructions (buried structures, utilities, old pile foundations, boulders) early in design
Complete existing utility location and potholing early to avoid contractor claims
Evaluate water table presence and seasonal variation; address bottom stability, softening, heaving, and dewatering needs
Geotechnical report should provide sufficient commentary for structural designer and estimator
sections.applicability: Constructability evaluation during foundation type selection, including excavation equipment, shoring, obstructions, and groundwater management.
